events.title: C language standardized
events.summary: ANSI ratified X3.159-1989 on December 14, 1989 — the first official standard for the C programming language.
events.about: ANSI C (C89/C90) was the first official contract for the C language — function prototypes, `const`, and a standard library (`stdio.h`, `stdlib.h`, etc.) that works the same on Unix, Windows, and embedded chips. Every modern C compiler still builds on this baseline.

narrative.whyChosen: C had been defined by a book (K&R), not a formal agreement. ANSI C was the first time compiler vendors signed off on one shared definition of the language.
narrative.whyImportant: A developer could write code on a Sun [workstation], ship it to a [PC], or flash it onto a microcontroller — and expect `printf`, `malloc`, and function calls to work the same way. That reliability is why C became the default for operating systems and device drivers.
narrative.problemSolved: Each vendor had extended C in incompatible ways. Code that compiled on one machine could fail on another, and there was no authority to settle what 'correct C' even meant.

events.title: PC Cyborg AIDS Trojan — first known ransomware
events.summary: In December 1989, thousands of [floppy disk]s mailed to AIDS conference attendees carried the [PC] Cyborg Trojan — the earliest documented ransomware, encrypting files and demanding payment by mail.
events.about: The "AIDS Information Introductory Disk" hid malware that counted reboots and eventually locked the system, demanding $189 to a Panama mailbox. It predated crypto-ransomware by decades but established the extortion pattern WannaCry and Colonial Pipeline attackers would later automate with Bitcoin and leaked exploits.

narrative.whyChosen: The AIDS Trojan is the first recorded ransomware attack in computing history.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved data hostage-taking worked before the internet made propagation trivial.
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing was solved — it introduced a threat model vendors ignored for twenty years.
